title: Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka have no respect for law, can breach peace and tranquility: Delhi SEM court
summary: A Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court on Monday said that Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka's conduct shows that they have no respect for the law and that there are serious concerns about them breaching peace and tranquillity. SEM Ritu Raj said that their assurance that they would not repeat the alleged conduct did not inspire confidence in light of their previous actions.The Court said that they showed "habitualness" by calling for protest at de-notified areas.Therefore, the Court extended their judicial custody by two days. "The application filed by IO [Investigating Officer] is supported by substantial material on record, raising serious concerns regarding the likelihood of breach of peace and disturbance of public tranquillity, which cannot be brushed aside without proper consideration," the Court said. Further, the SEM also rejected the sureties produced for Ranka and Das after finding them unfit.It noted a mismatch between the photograph on one of the sureties' bond and his Aadhaar card. The Court said that he [the surety] failed to produce another valid identity document and gave unsatisfactory answers. Meanwhile, according to the Court, the other surety could not provide basic details of Saurav Das. The court also found that neither surety could ensure the respondents’ presence before it. "The inquiry conducted revealed that both the Sureties has no control over the Respondents to produce them before the Court, which is primary essence of keeping Surety. No other Surety present at present. In such a situation, respondents are directed to furnish fresh Sureties," the Court recorded in its order. It has now listed the case for further consideration on October 21.Das and Ranka were detained by the Delhi Police on October 13 after they allegedly entered the barricaded Jantar Mantar site by climbing its gates. On October 14, they were sent to judicial custody for five days. As the custody ended today, they were produced before the SEM. The Delhi Police sought an extension of the custody. The same was allowed and the custody was extended by two more days.The CJP has been protesting alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.When Das and Ranka were produced before SEM today, the police told the court that they had breached an undertaking given before the SEM on October 11. It was stated that they called upon the public to assemble at Jantar Mantar, which has been de-notified as a protest site. The police further alleged that Das and Ranka repeatedly used social media to mobilise people for protests at non-designated locations, including Jantar Mantar and Connaught Place. The police officials also referred to an anonymous allegedly threatening WhatsApp communication received by the predecessor court, stating that a separate daily diary entry had been registered in connection with it. Opposing further detention, counsel for the respondents argued that they should be released immediately and assured the court that they would not repeat the alleged conduct. They also disputed the allegation that they had issued calls for protests after October 10.

title: YSR Congress moves Supreme Court alleging candidates blocked from filing nominations for municipal polls
summary: The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) has moved the Supreme Court alleging that poll violence blocked its candidates from filing nominations for the upcoming Andhra Pradesh's urban local body elections.The plea challenges an order passed by the Andhra Pradesh High Court refusing to extend the deadline for filing nominations.A vacation Bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana of the apex court will hear the plea on October 21. That is also the last date for withdrawal of candidature. Polling is scheduled for October 28.The party first moved the High Court on October 10, before the polls were notified, seeking secure additional nomination centres. A single-judge dismissed that plea on October 15.Subsequently, it moved the High Court flagging violence at nomination centres and seeking extension of deadline to file nominations.On October 18, a division bench of the High Court comprising Justices Ninala Jayasurya and Purushottam Kumar Chintalapudi rejected the party's plea for a one-day extension to file nominations. The High Court said that the time for filing nominations had expired and any direction to extend the same would amount to interference with the election process.This prompted the plea before the Supreme Court.As per the petition, there was violence at Punganur and Rayachoti on October 16, the first day of nominations. A candidate's papers were snatched and torn at Kadapa, and candidates in Tirupati were assaulted and prevented from reaching nomination centres. Nine Tirupati candidates have filed affidavits saying they were obstructed while trying to file their nominations.The petition argues that the principle of non-interference with elections is only a rule of judicial restraint and not an absolute bar on court's intervention.According to the plea,"In a situation where the democratic process is being thwarted, it is the bounden duty of the Constitutional Courts to step in and ensure that elections take place transparently and that no candidate is forced out of the race."Further, the expiry of time was itself the consequence of the obstruction complained of, and could not be a ground to deny relief, it has been contended.The plea has sought the following reliefs:- extension of the nomination period;- additional nomination centres with videography;- police protection for candidates; and- a stay on unopposed declarations.The petition was filed through advocate Mahfooz A Nazki.

title: Remembering the forgotten ones: Veteran Supreme Court lawyers recall AoRs, lawyers of yesteryear
summary: Doyens of the Supreme Court Bar recently reminisced the past, recalling lesser-known lawyers and Advocates-on-Record (AoRs) forgotten in days gone past.Moderated by Senior Advocate K Parameshwar, the discussion featured veteran Senior Advocates KK Venugopal, Raju Ramachandran and CS Vaidyanathan, as well as former Supreme Court Justice BP Singh.The panel also spoke about the agent system that was a precursor to the AoR mechanism, lawyers-turned-politicians and more.[Watch Video]Venugopal recalled the late R Gopalakrishnan, father of Senior Advocate Gopal Subramanium, who was his AoR right through from the 1960s until he passed away. The former Attorney General recounted an instance when Gopalakrishnan appeared in court despite suffering from internal bleeding.“He went about asking for adjournment on the last day, saying I have to have an operation. He told the Chief Justice that he was bleeding internally. And the Chief Justice was horrified. And nevertheless, he was trying to handle cases from court to court. Chief Justice said, Gopal, listen, do you know what you are doing with your life? You better go straight away. I won't listen to you for a moment.”The other names recalled by the panel included JB Dadachandji, Naunit Lal, Nuruddin Ahmed, AG Ratnaparkhi, Ganpat Rai, Arun Bahadur Saharya, RB Datar and BR Agarwala. Recalling Agarwala, Ramachandran said,“He was an avid book collector and he had a great work-life balance and he was a very efficient work manager…He would finish his work every day by around 6 o'clock, spend half an hour wandering around the second-hand bookshops of Connaught Place looking for a rare book to add to his collection. And he had an amazing private library...So among the books in his library was a fabulous collection of Kama Sutras in different languages published across the world. I didn't attempt to look, but I saw the shelf, which he proudly showed me!”Justice Singh spoke of a time when “agents” would manage cases in the Supreme Court before the formalised AoR system. The agents, who were not necessarily law graduates, would manage the cases. They corresponded with the lawyers, but they were not allowed to address the court, he said.“Then the judges decided that we should discontinue this agency and have AoRs When they said on record, they wanted to have a separate record of the advocates in the Supreme Court for the reason that we have cases from all over the country. So, they insisted that you have an office within the 10 kilometres of the Supreme Court. That was one. And two, that there should be law graduates. So, all those agents who were law graduates became advocates on record.”The panelists also discussed the relationship between senior advocates and AoRs back in the day, with Vaidyanathan recounting,“When there was criticism, something is missing, etc, they (senior advocates) would take it upon themselves. Unlike some of the seniors today, they were so generous and protective of the advocates on record. They would never expose the faults of the advocates on record.”The discussion moved on to lawyers-turned-politicians and the panelists listed Bengali lawyers who went to serve in positions with the government. They spoke of Somnath Chatterjee, Ashoke Sen, Siddhartha Shankar Ray, Sachindra Chaudhuri, Debi Prasad Pal and Sankar Ghose.Parameshwar then pointed out that Venugopal had two Cabinet Ministers – P Chidambaram and Rangarajan Kumaramangalam - working with him in chambers. Responding to a question on whether they indulged in politics during their time in chambers, Venugopal said,“No. See, when the emergency was declared, I was appearing for Karunanidhi challenging the dismissal of the government, alleging malafides against Indira Gandhi. They straight away had to leave my chambers…And at one time, when I was appearing in other emergency cases, when they were detained in Bangalore. When I went to Delhi, I was told that some IB man was inquiring as to which was my home and so on.Therefore, I was under the impression that it could be possible that along with all the other lawyers who had been detained, I could be with them. But I believe that these two former juniors of mine were responsible for telling the government that look, this will be a very wrong thing because so far as the Madras Bar is concerned, it has not been raising its voice against the Emergency. But if you do something, arrest him or raid him, then there may be a reaction.And I said, I don't mind the raid because all that they will find is an extra bottle of whisky, more than my permit permitted!”

title: Forgery by police in forgery case: Allahabad High Court orders perjury probe
summary: The Allahabad High Court has directed its Registrar General to probe the fabrication of an arrest memo submitted by the police in response to a habeas corpus petition alleging irregularities in the arrest of a man accused of forgery [Junaid and another v. State of UP and 4 Others]A Bench of Justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev found that the arrest memo submitted before the trial court at the time of remand was different from the one submitted by the police before the High Court.The Court found that the police added grounds of arrest to the arrest memo after the remand proceedings and "perhaps" after the filing of the habeas corpus petition."It is necessary to mention here that in the original arrest memo, this was never entered into by the I.O. and in order to perfect the arrest memo, perhaps after the habeas corpus petition was filed before this Court, by fabricating entries in Item Nos.12 and 13 of the second page of the arrest memo, which clearly reflect that fabricated document was placed before this Court along with the counter affidavit," the Court said.Justice Atul Sreedharan and Justice Achal SachdevThe Court was dealing with the habeas corpus plea moved by one Junaid, who was arrested by the Aligarh police on August 6. He alleged that the arrest memo provided to him did not have the grounds of arrest and thus his custody was in violation of the guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court.During the hearing, Junaid's counsel produced a certified copy of the arrest memo placed before the remand magistrate. He also pointed to the additions made to the arrest memo filed by the police in its response to the habeas corpus plea.On comparing the two documents, the High Court observed that the grounds of arrest mentioned in the original arrest memo were "perfunctory". It added the document filed before the High Court was fabricated."The certified copy reflects that the unfabricated original document that was placed before the Magistrate at the time of the remand. Thus, it is clear that the fabrication in the said document has been done by the police on a date after the remand proceedings and perhaps after the habeas corpus petition was filed," the Court said.The Court noted that the documents may have been fabricated by the investigating officer. Taking a serious note of the offence committed by the police, the Court passed the following direction:"This Court considers it necessary to direct the Registrar General of this Court to proceed under Section 379 of BNSS for cases mentioned in Section 215 of BNSS, as the offence has been committed in a judicial proceeding. After the inquiry, if the Registrar General is satisfied that prima facie, an offence relating to fabrication of documents and perjury has been committed before this Court, on the basis of perusal of the documents/records of this case, in such an eventuality, he shall do the needful and file a case before the Court of competent jurisdiction against those found prima facie involved in the offence." Concluding that the grounds of arrest given to the accused were inadequate, the Court ordered his release. Senior Advocate Mohit Singh and advocate Subir Lal represented the petitioner.[Read Order]

title: PIL in Calcutta High Court alleges State fraudulently issuing stamp papers to garner numbers for TMC rebel faction
summary: The Calcutta High Court on Tuesday sought a response from the West Bengal government to a public interest litigation (PIL) petition alleging that the State in cahoots with police and other authorities is fraudulently distributing stamp papers and forcefully obtaining signatures of Trinamool congress (TMC) members and others to support rebel members and leader of opposition Ritabrata Banerjee's faction [Surajit Mondal v. State of West Bengal and Ors.].A division bench of Chief Justice Ravindra Vithalrao Ghuge and Justice Shabbar Rashidi said that stamp papers can be sold only by licensed vendors and such sale must be properly recorded."Stamp papers can only be sold by licensed stamp vendors. The sale of stamp papers must be there in the register. Show us whether you are doing this," the Court said.The State said it will file a detailed response and sought time for the same.The court agreed and posted the case for further consideration on December 11. The petition before the Court was filed by one Surajit Mondal, an elected member of the Zilla Parishad in Hooghly.The dispute arose from opposition leader Ritabrata Banerjee's claim that his rebel faction is the original TMC party which entitles him to the "Flower and Grass" symbol used by Mamata Bnerjee's faction. Ritabrata Banerjee had broken away from Mamata Banerjee's TMC and earlier this year and has been claiming that he represents the real TMC since he has the support of more MLAs. He was later recognised as the leader of opposition by the speak of West Bengal assembly.The dispute over which faction is the real TMC is pending before the Election Commission of India (ECI) and signatures on stamp papers is crucial to proving which faction has greater numbers.This would thus affect the outcome of the dispute before ECI.According to the petition, the upper echelons of the State government have instructed local authorities across West Bengal to unlawfully order the distribution of stamp papers, and existing TMC members and others have been coerced to give their signatures for the cause of the rebel faction.Senior Advocate Kalyan Bandopadhyay, appearing for the petitioner, said that lakhs of stamp papers have been issued without making serialized entries of the issuance of the papers in the appropriate registers.He said that the Court should call for a report from the State detailing the entries of stamp papers in the requisite sub-registries.The State, on the other hand, challenged the maintainability of the PIL but sought time to seek instructions from the concerned departments. The Court then asked State to file its response.The issue pertaining to the maintainability of the petition remains to be argued at length. "Since the issue of maintainability has been raised, the Respondents are at liberty to file their specific objection with regard to the maintainability of the PIL, along with their reply, with proper pagination in continuation with the petition," the Court said in its order.Senior Advocate Kalyan Bandopadhyay and advocates Suman Sengupta, Anit Kumar Das, Ashish Dutta and Rahul Kumar Singh appeared for the petitionerGovernment Pleader DN Ray with advocates Anindya Basu, Pradip Mukherjee, Indradeep Pal and Bikash Kumar Sriwastav represented the State.[Read Order]

title: Allahabad High Court asks Centre, RBI to frame guidelines to deal with bank accounts of persons in coma
summary: The Allahabad High Court has asked the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to consider framing guidelines to deal with bank accounts held by persons in a coma [Parveen Jahan v State of UP and Another]A bench of Justice Ajit Kumar and Justice Garima Prasad expressed concern that the dependents of such patients are left without any legal remedy, as they cannot access the funds held in their bank accounts,The Court directed the Central government and the RBI to disclose what they propose to do in this regard or place on record any existing guidelines to attend to such cases of special nature. “Some sort of legislation from the competent legislature or even the guidelines necessary from the Reserve Bank of India regulating the nationalised bank and subsidiary banks to the nationalised banks for providing necessary mechanism as to how the money lying in the savings bank account of such patients can be released in favour of the dependents. The Central Government, therefore, has to come up with its stand on the issue in black and white. We also need Reserve Bank of India to give its response on the above issue,” the Court said.Justice Ajit Kumar and Justice Garima PrashadThe Court was dealing with a petition filed by a woman seeking to withdraw money lying in the bank account of her husband, who was in a coma. The man died during the pendency of the plea.Considering the larger question raised in the case, the Court asked the Central government and RBI to address the issue at the earliest.“The Reserve Bank of India and the Central Government will have to file their respective affidavits, failing which the Court will be compelled to summon the responsible officers of both the Central Government as well as Reserve Bank of India,” the Court said on October 8.The matter will be heard next on November 6. In the meantime, the Court said that the State can consider enforcement of the guidelines framed by the Kerala High Court in Shobha Gopalakrishnan v. State of Kerala. It said the Chief Secretary must come up with something concrete and substantial at his level. “We make it clear that if the Chief Secretary does not come up with such solution in black and white, he will have to appear in person before this Court on the next date fixed,” the Court said.Advocate Raj Kumar Dhama represented the petitioner.[Read Order]

title: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka move Delhi High Court against judicial custody
summary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka have approached the Delhi High Court against a special executive magistrate (SEM) court order sending them to judicial custody till October 21. They have alleged that their continued detention violates their fundamental right to liberty.The CJP's legal head, Ratna Singh, said they would be seeking an urgent hearing and would request the Court to get the matter listed today.Notably, the Delhi Police detained Das and Ranka on October 13 after they allegedly entered the barricaded Jantar Mantar site by climbing its gates. On October 14, they were sent to judicial custody for five days. On October 19, the custody was extended for two more days. In its October 19 order, the SEM court said that Das and Ranka's conduct showed that they have no respect for the law and that there are serious concerns about them breaching peace and tranquillity. It held that their assurance that they would not repeat the alleged conduct did not inspire confidence in light of their previous actions.The Court said that they showed "habitualness" by calling for protest at de-notified areas.Further, the SEM also rejected the sureties produced for Ranka and Das after finding them unfit. It noted a mismatch between the photograph on one of the sureties' bond and his Aadhaar card. The Court said that he [the surety] failed to produce another valid identity document and gave unsatisfactory answers. The other surety could not provide basic details of Saurav Das. The Court also found that neither surety could ensure the respondents’ presence before it. Das and Ranka have now approached the High Court against their custody.In this petition, Das and Ranka have contended that they have remained in custody for six days despite repeatedly furnishing sureties.They have argued that the magistrate wrongly extended their judicial custody under Section 135(3) BNSS on the ground that they had defaulted in executing the required bond, despite their sureties having been produced in accordance with law.The plea states that the SEM order mechanically relies on the police's application without recording an independent assessment of the circumstances warranting continued custody. Further, they argue that a protest at a denotified site is, at its highest, a question of regulation, not a threat to public order. "That a restraint on the liberty of the Petitioners founded on an apprehension of breach of tranquillity or public order and attributed to them, must satisfy the test of Article 19(3) of the Constitution," the plea states.On the issue of surety, they rely on a 2018 Delhi High Court judgment in Aldanish Rein v State of NCT of Delhi to argue that a person should be released on a personal bond while verification of the sureties is pending.The plea further alleges that the magistrate rejected their sureties on grounds that they could not guarantee the petitioners’ appearance before the court and could not recall their parentage. The CJP activists contend that Section 140 BNSS permits rejection of a surety only if the person is found unfit for the bond. They have also argued that the magistrate failed to specify the number of sureties, the bond amount and the duration of the bond, as required under Section 130 BNSS.

title: Calcutta High Court dismisses CPI(M)'s plea to halt removal of temporary book stall
summary: The Calcutta High Court on Tuesday dismissed the Communist Party of India (Marxist)'s [CPI(M)] plea to halt the removal and dismantling of a temporary book stall near the Jadavpur coffee house during Durga Puja despite making the requisite application and paying a fee to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) [Communist Party of India (Marxist) v. State of West Bengal & Ors.]. Justice Partha Pratim Roy observed that making the requisite application and paying the fee to the local authorities for operating a temporary book stall is not enough without explicit permission for operating such a stall."In view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Division Bench in MAT 1881 of 2026, a person who approaches the Court will have to be first established whether the said party has a permission for erecting a stall or not. Therefore, the protection as sought for by the petitioner requires establishing, that they had a valid permission to run the bookstall. In the present case, such permission is absent. In view of the law declared by the Hon’ble Division Bench, the writ petitioner is not entitled to any relief as prayed for," the Court said.CPI(M) moved the Court after some people, allegedly belonging to the KMC and accompanied by a large police contingent and a bulldozer, attempted to remove the stall on October 17.CPI(M) had been operating the temporary book stall in front of the Jadavpur coffee house during Durga Puja for the last 49 years.Keeping up with the same practice, they applied for permission to set up the book stall to the office of Assistant Director SWM-I, Borough – X, Kolkata Municipal Corporation. A fee amounting to ₹3,208 was also paid to the concerned KMC department in this regard. A letter to that effect was also sent to the concerned officer-in-charge of the nearby police station . After examining the facts of the case, the Court observed, "Running of the aforesaid bookstall an application for permission was also made on 19th September, 2026 and an amount was also deposited with the Kolkata Municipal Corporation for grant of such permission. Therefore, by the aforesaid acts of the petitioner, itself proves that obtaining permission is mandatory before running of the bookstall, and therefore, such application was made. The receipt showing of depositing money was accepted subject to police permission. In the present case, it is admitted fact that no permission was granted to the petitioner for running the bookstall."Placing reliance on a similar order, Justice Roy dismissed the case holding that the CPI(M) was not entitled to the reliefs prayed for since no explicit permission was granted. Advocate Abhijit Mondal appeared for CPI(M). [Read Order]

title: Lawyer can't be faulted for asking NCLT to upload its order on website: NCLAT
summary: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) recently held that an advocate cannot be faulted for sending an email to the court master of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) requesting that a judicial order passed by NCLT be uploaded on its website [Mrinal Vs Hynite]The order copy had remained unavailable for 18 days after the pronouncement.A bench of Judicial Member Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan and Technical Member Naresh Salecha deleted the adverse remarks made by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) against advocate Mrinal Harsh Vardhan, who had emailed the NCLT court master asking that the order be uploaded.The NCLAT found that the email was polite and merely reflected the advocate's anxiety to obtain the order."Naturally when the order which was pronounced in the open Court on 05.06.2026 could not be uploaded for 18 days, we do not find any error in the act of the Appellant in sending an e-mail to the Court Master of the concerned Bench, requesting only for the uplodation of the order which was admittedly pronounced in the open Court on 05.06.2026," the NCLAT observed.The case arose from insolvency proceedings concerning Hynite Farms Private Limited.On June 5, the NCLT pronounced an order concerning the approval of a resolution plan. However, the order was not uploaded for several days.Vardhan, who represented the Resolution Professional, subsequently emailed the Court Master requesting that the same be published on the NCLT website.The email explained that the order was urgently required to implement the approved resolution plan, particularly in view of Supreme Court directions requiring coordination with the NOIDA authority.However, the NCLT made adverse observations concerning the advocate's conduct in its orders dated June 5 and July 6.Aggrieved, Vardhan approached the NCLAT, arguing that the email was neither scandalous nor improper. He also submitted that the remarks could adversely affect his professional reputation and had been made without hearing him.The respondents did not oppose his request.After examining the email, the NCLAT agreed that the advocate had done nothing wrong."We have also perused the e-mail which clearly shows that the language of the same is quite soft," the NCLAT observed.It also noted that the order had not been uploaded for 18 days despite being pronounced in open court.Accordingly, the NCLAT expunged the adverse observations while clarifying that its decision could not be relied upon in other pending contempt of court proceedings.The appellant was represented by advocates Chitranshul Sinha, Aaditya Mishra, Srishti Aggarwal and Aayushi Kiran.Advocate Sajeev Deora appeared for the Resolution Professional while advocates Rishi Singhal and Tannu Rana represented Hynite Farms.[Read Judgment]

title: Police misusing NDPS Act in cases involving codeine cough syrup: Patna High Court
summary: The Patna High Court recently criticised the police for routinely registering cases under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act when cough syrups containing codeine are seized, despite the drug falling within the permissible concentration limits prescribed by the Central government [Bharat Kumar v. State of Bihar].Justice Ashok Kumar Pandey termed the invocation of the stringent NDPS Act in such matters strange, adding that such cases need only be dealt with under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act."Cough syrup containing codeine is only a Schedule H drug for which the shopkeeper has to maintain a register and he must be a licensed one. Such types of cases should be filed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. It is only a violation of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, whereas the police is invariably misusing the procedure," the Court said.Justice Ashok Kumar PandeyThe Court made the observation while dealing with a bail plea by one Bharat Kumar. Kumar was arrested in May 2026 in an NDPS case following the recovery of 484 litres of codeine-based cough syrup from a pick-up van in Bihar's Khagaria district.Kumar maintained that he had merely been standing near the vehicle and had no connection with either the vehicle or the seized cough syrup.His counsel further argued that no contraband had been recovered from his possession, that he had no criminal antecedents and that a similarly placed co-accused had already been granted bail.His counsel also invoked a Central government notification dated November 14, 1985, under which certain codeine preparations are excluded from the definition of manufactured drugs under the NDPS Act.The exemption applies to preparations containing not more than 100 milligrams of codeine per dosage unit and a concentration not exceeding 2.5 per cent, provided other prescribed conditions, including their established therapeutic use, are satisfied.Meanwhile, the State opposed the bail application, relying on the Supreme Court's judgment in Hira Singh v. Union of India, which held that the entire weight of a mixture containing a narcotic drug must be considered while determining whether the seized quantity of material falls within the commercial quantity threshold. Under Section 37 of the NDPS Act, where the seized material is of commercial quantity, bail cannot be granted unless the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of the offence and that the accused is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.The Court, however, noted that where the preparation itself does not qualify as a narcotic drug, the question of determining whether the recovered substance is of a commercial quantity or not would not arise. In this regard, it also noted the bail applicant's argument that the cough syrup recovered in the present case contained less than 2.5 per cent codeine, meaning that its seizure attracted only the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, not the NDPS Act. It proceeded to grant Kumar bail. "Before parting, it is very strange that the cases where cough syrups containing codeine are recovered, the police is invariably filing cases under N.D.P.S. Act whereas in view of the notification of Central Government (supra) concentration of codeine being less than 2.5 %, the quantity does not come under the ambit of contraband," the Court added in its October 1 order. Advocate Vijay Kishore Bharti represented the bail applicant.Additional Public Prosecutor Surendra Prasad Singh appeared for the State.[Read Judgment]

title: Only Supreme Court can say its judgment will not be cited as precedent: Delhi High Court
summary: The Delhi High Court recently held that only the Supreme Court can give a caveat that its judgment will not be cited as a precedent. A Division Bench of Justices C Hari Shankar and Vinod Kumar said that such a power is not available to any other court. “This caveat is, therefore, unique to the Supreme Court, as its decisions are constitutionally binding by virtue of Article 141 of the Constitution of India,” the Bench explained. It said that even if the facts of a case are similar to those in an earlier Supreme Court judgment, a lower court cannot treat that judgment as binding precedent if the Supreme Court itself has clarified that it should not apply in such circumstances. In such cases, the binding effect of Article 141 of the Constitution would not apply.Further, the Bench reasoned that if other courts say that their judgments will not be cited as a precedent, it could result in a situation in which similarly placed litigants would receive different treatment. “Ex facie, this would be impermissible,” the Court added. Justice C Hari Shankar and Justice Vinod KumarThe High Court rendered these observations as it upheld a Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) order. The CAT had granted a retired Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) scientist ante-dated in situ promotion under the Flexible Complementing Scheme (FCS). The Court ruled that his further promotion must still be assessed.Notably, the Central government had challenged the CAT order before the High Court, arguing that the recruitment rules and Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) memoranda bar retrospective promotion. It was also that the FCS is a merit-based scheme requiring screening, interview and committee assessment.However, the High Court rejected this argument. It held that the case was covered by a Supreme Court’s and its own ruling in Nakul Dev v Union of India. Pertinently, it was the Nakul Dev judgment of the High Court which carried a caveat that it could not be cited as precedent. The Central government had relied on this judgment. CGSC Balendu Shekhar with advocates Krishna Chaitanya and Divyansh Singh Dev appeared for Union of India. title: Bombay High Court halts release of Sonakshi Sinha-starrer Tu Hai Meri Kiran
summary: The Bombay High Court has restrained the theatrical release of Hindi film "Tu Hai Meri Kiran" until co-producer Echelon Productions deposits ₹8.85 crore along with 15 percent interest [AND Movie Products LLP v. Echelon Productions & Ors.].Justice Amit Borkar passed the interim order on October 19 under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act on a plea moved by co-producer AND Movie Products LLP. The film, starring Sonakshi Sinha and Zaheer Iqbal, was slated for release on October 23.Justice Amit BorkarAND Movie moved the Court contending that it had invested ₹8.85 crore under a March 2024 co-production agreement, which Echelon Productions failed to refund despite an expired timeline and a dishonoured cheque. In defence, Echelon contended that AND Movie had acquiesced to the film’s release by actively collaborating on promotional posts on Instagram.The Court rejected this contention, observing that social media promotion cannot be construed as a waiver of financial claims or exploitation rights.“There is a difference between agreeing to promote the announcement of a film and agreeing to give up the contractual right to get back the investment. In the same way, accepting an Instagram collaboration post is not the same thing as giving prior consent to the terms of a commercial exploitation agreement. Both acts are different and their effect may be different,” the order said. The Court further clarified that subsequent conduct cannot override express contractual terms:“The conduct of the parties may help the court in understanding their agreement. But unless there is sufficient material to show that they intended to change the agreement, such conduct cannot be used to remove an obligation which has been written in it,” the judge observed. Consequently, the Bench directed Echelon to deposit ₹8.85 crore with 15 percent interest within three working days as security before proceeding with the release of the film.Further, Echelon was ordered to disclose all third-party exploitation agreements and restore the agreed producer credits within forty-eight hours.Senior advocate Ashish Kamat with advocates Rashmin Khandekar, Ashwin Bhadang, Arpit Choudhary, Krunal Mehta, Karen Koya, Akshata Modi and Varun Dhond briefed by King Stubb & Kasiva appeared for AND Movie.Advocates Anand Mohan, Lavin Hirani, Clint G Thattil and Vikramaditya Chavan appeared for Echelon Productions. title: Kerala High Court upholds 10-year jail term for man who raped 73-year-old woman on pretext of removing evil spirits
summary: The Kerala High Court recently upheld the conviction and 10-year prison sentence of a man who raped a 73-year-old woman in Thrissur on the pretext that he was removing evil spirits from her body [Muhammed v State of Kerala].Justice A Badharudeen dismissed an appeal filed by on Muhammad challenging his trial court conviction for the offences of rape and sexual harassment under the Indian Penal Code (IPC).In its October 12 ruling, the High Court held that the rape survivor's testimony was sufficient to establish the guilt of the convict, despite discrepancies concerning the date of the incident and a delay of 19 days in reporting the crime."The learned Special Judge is right in holding that the accused committed the offences punishable under Sections 354 A(1)(i) and 376(1) of IPC," the Court held.It also cancelled the bail earlier given to the convict and directed him to surrender immediately before the trial court to serve out his jail sentence.Justice A BadharudeenThe case arose from an incident that took place on October 8, 2022, when Muhammed (accused) visited the rape survivor's house after she contacted him on her son's advice.According to the prosecution, the accused, who was already acquainted with the survivor, had visited her house on three earlier occasions. He claimed that evil spirits were present in her body and offered to remove them.Under the guise of curing her ailments, he touched her breasts as well as her private parts and even inserted his finger into her vagina.A trial court convicted him of rape and sexual harassment. It sentenced him to 10 year of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of ₹1 lakh for rape. The court also sentenced him to 3 years of imprisonment with a fine of ₹25,000 for the offence of sexual harassment. Both jail sentences were to run concurrently. The accused challenged the trial court's September 2024 ruling before the High Court. He argued that the survivor had initially stated that the crime had occurred on October 7, 2022, but later changed the date to October 8. The accused further relied on the testimony of the survivor's son to suggest that the survivor had falsely implicated him because of a property dispute and that there was a delay in filing the complaint.The Court noted that the son himself had differences with his mother and, therefore, his testimony could not be used to disbelieve her account of the sexual assault.It also found that the survivor had corrected the date in an additional statement given to the police and held that such a discrepancy did not undermine her testimony, which was supported by telephone records showing three calls between her and the accused on October 8.The Court also held that the absence of injuries was not sufficient to discredit the survivor's testimony. It relied on a doctor's explanation that the medical examination of the survivor was conducted 20 days after the incident and that any injuries caused by the assault could have healed by then.Further, it rejected the argument that there was a delay in registering the First Information Report (FIR), noting that the survivor had waited to consult her children before approaching the police.Finding no reason to interfere with the trial court's decision to convict the accused man, the High Court proceeded to dismiss his appeal.Advocates Balamurali KP, Manu Tom, Renil Iqubal K, Haripriya M, Amal C Peter, Mohammed Ashiq RS and MB Soori appeared for the appellant.Public Prosecutor MA Shihab represented the State.[Read Judgment]

summary: ASG Sharma now refers to Section 130 of BNSS.Court: "Likely to commit" is based on the information received... Court: He is saying it is premature.Court: The question is that could it (show cause notice) be in the nature of a judgement? Constitution Bench makes it clear that at every stage you have to give reasons in writing.Gopal S refers to 7 judge Supreme Court bench in Madhu Limaye case.Gopal S: Stage 1 is substance; stage 2 is the inquiry.Gopal S refers to Section 135 BNSS.Court: So your third argument would be no independent opinion of the SEM? Gopal S: Yes, in fact, there is no opinion at all.Gopal S: The notice is ex facie constitutionally wrong and legally wrong.Court: The subjective satisfaction I cannot go into unless the subjective satisfaction is such that... There is no question of incitement to violence, breaking of any law, breach peace, upsetting public tranquility, inviting congregation in order to commit any offence.Bench: Your arguments are on the wordings of Section 130 and 126. Gopal S: On October 15 there is a press conference by the petitioner in Press Club. On October 16 at 4 PM a post is put up. This was a reaction to the fact that Jantar Mantar was suddenly denotified.Gopal S refers to Jantar Mantar on a map.Gopal S: She has been asking for reforms. title: Karnataka High Court calls for integrated database of criminal cases
summary: The Karnataka High Court has directed the State police to verify the latest status of criminal proceedings before issuing notices proposing to open or continue rowdy sheets against individuals [Anthony David Vs State of Karnataka].Pertinently, Justice Suraj Govindaraj called for the creation of an integrated digital database of criminal cases to prevent police authorities from initiating proceedings on the basis of outdated or incomplete records.The Court said that digital systems such as the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS), the Inter-operable Criminal Justice System (ICJS) and the e-Courts database could be integrated to provide police officers with updated information on criminal proceedings. It requested the Inspector General of Police of Police Computer Wing to examine the feasibility of developing an integrated digital platform or upgrading existing infrastructure to draw information from CCTNS, ICJS, the e-Courts database and other available government databases."Such platform shall, to the extent technologically feasible, draw information from the CCTNS, the ICJS, the e-Courts database and such other governmental databases as may be available, so as to provide a single-window view of the status of every criminal case relating to a person," the Court said.Justice Suraj GovindrajThe directions were issued while allowing a petition filed by 26-year-old Anthony David J alias Kutti, who challenged a July 16 notice proposing to enter his name in the Rowdy Register on the ground that an FIR was pending against him.He submitted that an earlier notice proposing to open a rowdy sheet against him had been quashed by the High Court on July 22, 2024. He further pointed out that the criminal proceedings arising from the same case had culminated in his acquittal on July 10, 2025.Accepting his submissions, the Court said there existed no factual or legal basis for either opening or continuing a rowdy sheet in his name of the petitioner after his acquittal in the only criminal case. It thus quashed the notice.The Court observed that the case was not an isolated instance as police authorities repeatedly issue notices proposing to open or continue rowdy sheets solely on the basis of registered criminal cases, without verifying their subsequent status.While acknowledging that rowdy sheets may serve as an administrative measure to maintain public order and monitor habitual offenders, the Court cautioned that they could adversely affect an individual's reputation, dignity, liberty, employment, business and social standing, apart from exposing them to continuous police surveillance.“Such a measure, therefore, cannot be resorted to in a routine or mechanical manner,” it said.The Court emphasised that the competent authority must be satisfied, on the basis of existing and relevant material, that the legal requirements for opening or continuing a rowdy sheet had been fulfilled.“Once such information is available electronically, there can be little justification for initiating proceedings on the basis of outdated or incomplete information” the Court said.The Court directed the Director General of Police and Inspector General of Police to issue administrative instructions making verification of the current status of criminal proceedings mandatory before issuing a notice proposing to open or continue a rowdy sheet.“Such verification and recording of satisfaction shall constitute an essential prerequisite before any notice is issued,” the Court directed.The judgment was passed on July 28. The matter was listed on August 25 and October 15 for compliance. However, at the request of the State Government the matter was adjourned to October 29.Advocate B Madhusudhan Adiga appeared for the petitionerAdditional Government Advocate Saritha Kulkarni represented the State.[Read Judgment]

title: Saurav Ganguly moves Delhi High Court against movie Doosra, claims rights over Lord's shirtless celebration
summary: The Delhi High Court on Thursday refused to pass any order on a plea by former India cricket captain Sourav Ganguly’s plea to stay the release of the film “Doosra”. Justice Dinesh Bhatt said the case will be heard tomorrow (Thursday). The movie is scheduled to be released in theatres tomorrow.Justice Bhatt made it clear that he has not stopped the release of the film in theatres. "I have said no stay, so the film can go on," Justice Bhatt said.Ganguly and film production house Luv Films LLP have approached the Delhi High Court seeking to restrain the release of the film citing exploitation of the former's live events, particularly his captaincy in the NatWest cricket series final and his shirtless celebration at Lord's.They have alleged unauthorised commercial exploitation of Ganguly’s personality rights and infringement of the production house’s exclusive contractual rights over his proposed biopic.Ganguly and Luv Films have sought an injunction against the film’s theatrical, digital and other releases, as well as the circulation of promotional material allegedly using Ganguly’s name, image, likeness and iconic cricketing moments without authorisation.According to the suit, Ganguly entered into an agreement with Luv Films on August 5, 2021, granting the production house exclusive rights to develop, produce and commercially exploit audiovisual content, including a biographical film based on his life and cricketing career.The suit states that Luv Films has made substantial investments in the authorised biopic, titled Dada – The Sourav Ganguly Story, which is scheduled for release on May 14, 2027.It adds that the trailer and promotional campaign for Doosra, launched on October 12, prominently refer to Ganguly’s leadership of the Indian cricket team and its historic victory in the 2002 NatWest Series final at Lord’s. This includes his shirtless celebration on the Lord’s balcony.They contend that these references are being used to generate commercial interest by capitalising on Ganguly’s identity and reputation, potentially creating an impression that he is associated with or has endorsed the film.The suit also cites an October 13 interview in which Doosra director Abhinay Deo discussed how the 2002 NatWest final and milestones in Ganguly’s career influenced the film’s fictional character, Tara.Ganguly's counsel told the Court that the movie is a violation of his personality rights and no license was taken from the former cricketer for the movie. The counsel stated that Ganguly is a "pseudo hero" for the film and almost a third of the trailer is Ganguly footage. It was also stated that the director of the movie referred to Ganguly in an interview. However, the counsel appearing for the movie makers said that it is not a biopic on Ganguly. The Court was told that the story is of a girl from Rajasthan who draws inspiration from Ganguly. The counsel added that a licence for use of footage of NatWest series was taken from Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) and that the player [Ganguly] has no right over such footage.The suit by Ganguly and Luv Films was filed through advocates Jaya Goyal and Manpreet Kaur of Neo Juris. Senior Advocate Balbir Singh with advocates Ameet Naik, Madhu Gadodia, Megha Chandra, Dhruv Anand, Sakshi Dube, Unnati Gambani and Khushi Agarwal appeared for defendant Masjda Sajeh. Senior Advocate Saurabh Kirpal with advocates Ameet Naik, Madhu Gadodia, Sanjeevi Seshadri, Dhruv Anand, Sakshi Dube, Unnati Gambani and Khushi Agarwal represented the director and the producer of the film.

Parents or police can't force adult woman to return home against her wishes: Kerala High Court
summary: The Kerala High Court has observed that an adult woman cannot be compelled to return to her parental home against her wishes by the police or her parents on a missing person complaint. [XXX v State of Kerala & ors]Justice Bechu Kurian Thomas made the observation while disposing of a petition filed by a 22-year-old woman who alleged that police were repeatedly summoning her to the police station after she left her family home to pursue her education.In a judgment delivered on September 26, the judge said that a woman above the age of 18 has the right to make her own decisions, including where she wishes to decide. "Notwithstanding the above, since the petitioner asserts that she is now residing at Thrissur and does not intend to go back to her parental home, she, being a major, is entitled to take decisions about her. Neither her parents nor the police can interfere with such freedom to decide," the judge said.Justice Bechu Kurian ThomasThe petitioner moved the Court contending that her family had arranged her marriage without her consent and that she later left her husband's house after he did not meet her needs.She returned to her paternal home, but in April 2026, she left her paternal home after her father refused to allow her to continue her education. She then began living in Thrissur.Following this, her mother filed a missing person complaint at the Kattakada Police Station in Thiruvananthapuram.The petitioner alleged that police officers repeatedly harassed her by asking her to appear at the station and feared that they were trying to force her to return to her parents against her wishes.The police denied the allegations of harassment and informed the Court that they contacted her only to investigate the missing person complaint.Considering the submissions, the Court clarified that the police were duty-bound to investigate a complaint once a case had been registered and found no reason to presume that the police were harassing the petitioner.Accordingly, the Court directed the petitioner to appear before the Chavakkad Police Station at Thrissur for recording her whereabouts details and whether she wished to return to her parental home.It also directed that she could not be forced to return if she wished to stay in Thrissur and asked the Chavakkad Police Station to communicate the information to Kattakada Police Station for completing their investigation on the missing person complaint.Advocate VA Johnson (Varikkappallil) appeared for the petitioner.Government pleader Laya Mary Joseph represented the state.[Read Judgment]

title: Nothing wrong in call for regime change: Neha Bora to Delhi High Court in SEM notice case
summary: All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora told the Delhi High Court on Thursday that in a democracy, there is nothing wrong in making a call for a regime change.Bora was responding to the argument by Delhi Police that they (Bora has been referred to by they/ them pronouns) were part of the gathering in which a call was made for change of regime."Joint sitting with CJP leaders and Prashant Bhushan where it was said ye regime change ki ladai hai aur ham regime change karwa ke rahenge. She was part of the same gathering," the law officer for Delhi Police contended."There is nothing wrong with regime change in a democracy," Bora's counsel said."Do we need to go into that?" the Court asked."Regime change will (have to) happen by votes, not by lumpen elements congregating in New Delhi," the Delhi Police replied.The Court was hearing a plea filed by Bora challenging a notice issued to them by the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) directing them to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 and maintain peace.The hearing transpired before Justice Subramonium Prasad who reserved his verdict after hearing all parties at length.The order will passed tomorrow at 6 pm, the judge said.During the hearing, Bora also contended that there is no requirement under law to seek prior permission for hoisting the national flag.Justice Subramonium PrasadThe notice under challenge was issued by the Delhi Police to Bora on October 18, directing them to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) on October 19. The notice directed Bora to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 with a surety to “maintain peace during the period of inquiry” against them.According to Bora’s plea, the notice dated October 17 was issued by the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) under Sections 126 and 130, read with Section 135(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), citing apprehensions of breach of public peace and tranquillity.Bora was detained on October 16 while attending a gathering at Mandi House. Bora has alleged that they were taken to an undisclosed location and subsequently to RK Puram police station, where they were held overnight before being released at 6 AM the following day. They received the SEM notice on October 18.The notice cited allegations of sloganeering at Mandi House, repeated protests around Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, and allegedly instigating people to participate in a protest at Connaught Place.However, according to Bora's plea, the notice does not disclose any material establishing a likelihood of breach of peace or identify a specific event or period during which such a breach is apprehended.The petition also disputed the allegation concerning the Connaught Place protest. Bora argued that their call was for a peaceful gathering at Mandi House at 5 pm on October 16, where they were subsequently detained.Bora has alleged that the proceedings amount to an attempt to curb peaceful dissent and violate their fundamental rights to freedom of speech, assembly and personal liberty.Neha Bora argumentsSenior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for Bora, submitted that all calls made by them were for peaceful protests."The facts are that over a period of time certain protests have arisen in the country as it the want against what the government does. As far as my client is concerned there has been no exhortation to violence it has been entirely peaceful. She has been asking for reforms. Over time, she has put out tweets and exhorted people to join," it was submitted.Sankaranarayanan referred to the press conference held by Bora on October 15 in response to the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a protest site.He sought to distinguish the protest that happened at Connaught Place from the one which Bora had called for at Mandi House."There is no question of incitement to violence, breaking of any law, breach peace, upsetting public tranquility, inviting congregation in order to commit any offence. On the evening of October 16, when she caled for the protest when she goes to the Mandi House area, she comes to be detained barely 10-15 minutes. At that time she had not been guilty fo any offence. The only thing that happened was that she raised some slogans and she was detained. We believe that it is completely illegal detention. The protest at Connaught Place was organised by some other organisation. She had given a call for (protest at) Mandi House. It has now become a practise that when people are protesting, they are taken away, not allowed to get in touch with lawyer, nothing," Sankaranarayanan argued.Senior Advocate Gopal SankaranarayananHe also highlighted how the special executive magistrate issuing the notice is also an police officer."It is admitted that there was a direction by senior officers to initiate the procedure under Section 126. It is relevant because the SEM here is also an ACP," it was pointed out.He further flagged errors in the notice and maintained that no permission is required to hoist the national flag."I did not say anything about CP. It says, 'hoist the national flag without permission'.. I am surprised anyone can say this. No permission is needed to hoist the national flag," Sankaranarayanan said.He contended that a notice directing execution of bond can be issued only after an inquiry into the necessity of the same and not mechanically."First, it [notice] is cut and paste which vitiates it. Second, even for an interim bond an inquiry is essential. The magistrate could not have birthed the idea of a personal bond until the inquiry into the necessity of the bond was complete," Sankaranarayanan submitted."When you read Section 135, I want to know what is your input on proviso after 135 (3). read the first proviso. How do you see 135... I am saying this in your favour. How do you read this proviso in respect to what is being transpired now. Is it not better for you to 135 inquiry to be completed?" the bench asked.The Court said that it cannot go into the subjective satisfaction of the SEM."The subjective satisfaction i cannot go into unless the subjective satisfaction is such that.... The compass is exceedingly narrow," the judge remarked."The notice is ex facie constitutionally wrong and legally wrong," Sankaranarayanan argued."So your third argument would be no independent opinion of the SEM?" the Court asked. "Yes, in fact, there is no opinion at all," Sankaranarayanan said.He said that he will not go into the merits of the allegations in the notice and that if that were to be done, then the remedy would lie elsewhere."If I were to engage with the merits of the allegations, then my remedy is obviously not here. I am not engaging. I am saying compliance with law. That entitles me to come here under Article 226," it was submitted.Neha Bora No permission is needed to hoist the national flag.Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Chetan Sharma, appearing for Delhi Police, rebutted Bora's arguments. The Court asked the ASG whether the SEM should not have conducted an inquiry before issuing the notice to Bora."Let's assume someone tells the magistrate that X was there shouting slogans... And on that basis, he issues a 126 BNSS notice. So therefore, without making an inquiry, he gives a 126 notice to file a bond without even finding out that x may not even be there at all and on that very date there are press reports that x was at some other place giving a speech; then is it not necessary for the magistrate to do an independent search that the information received is credible enough to take an action?" the bench queried."Two things need to be kept in mind. The entire argument proceeds on two aspects. One, procedurally there is no challenge. His case is 130, the requirements in 130 and 126 do not meet. So it is a challenge to the substance, not the procedure. The challenge to 130 is based on demurrer that there are some penal consequences," the ASG said.The Court asked whether receipt of any information about likelihood of a crime would be sufficient to issue a Section 126 notice."According to you, receipt of information 'likely to commit'?" the Court asked."Likely to commit what? Not the crime in traditional sense but a breach of peace and that may probably occasion a breach.. This has some connotation... This is subjective satisfaction as wide it can get," Sharma replied."'Likely to commit' is based on the information received. The question is, whether there is an application of mind that the information received leads to a subjective satisfaction that there is 'likely to commit'," the judge asked.The Court said that in cases relating to detention, the only safeguard for citizens is the procedure laid down by the law."In a matter where liberty is under challenge, the only safeguard available to a citizen is the procedure, the requirement. The only safeguard is the requirement of the law to be met," the Court said.The ASG said that Section 126 and 130 of the BNSS have to be read together."If there is a likelihood that somebody may commit breach of peace, Section 126 BNSS kicks in with Section 130 BNSS. They can't be disjoined. Such technical splitting will take away the essence of public tranquillity and breach of peace. Therefore, sometimes the law enjoins you," the ASG contended.ASG Chetan SharmaThe Court said that it will need time to write its judgment and urged the government not to act upon the notice in the meanwhile."ASG Sir, just a small request, we will require a bit more time to write the judgment. Saturday, Sunday I am not in station, the hearing will finish today. I will write the judgment by Tuesday. The only request is till Tuesday, hold your hands," the judge said."It does not sound good that a court is seeking adjournment. I will take it on myself that we are seeking adjournment," Sankaranarayanan said.ASG Sharma maintained that the notice was based on likelihood of breach of peace and cannot be assailed on the ground of technicality."There is a likelihood of breach of peace. Don't leave it to a technicality... All mayhem may have broken loose in the capital of the city. Because this is preventive in nature so that law would land its weight to the way parliament envisaged it to be," the ASG argued.Regarding Bora's arguments that the notice was factually incorrect since she was had not given any call for protest at Connaught Place but only at Mandi House, the ASG said,"Their argument that their call was only for Mandi House and not CP and that no 163 BNSS was in force is false. There was 163 BNSS. Police was outnumbered, she ran. She dodges. She was stopped, she did not stop. She ran towards CP."Besides Sankaranarayanan, advocates Abhik Chimni, Moksha Sharma, Ayan Dasgupta Samarendra, Pranjal Abrol and Gurupal Singh also appeared for Bora.[Read Live Coverage]Delhi High Court to hear today AISA President Neha Bora's plea challenging the notice issued by the Delhi SEM directing her to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 and maintain peace.Justice Subramonium Prasad will hear the matter at 2:30 PM. @neha_aisa @aisa_official_ pic.twitter.com/mlYiuvQMbY— Bar and Bench (@barandbench) October 22, 2026

title: UK Court of Appeal rejects India's challenge to arbitration over Andhra Pradesh bauxite project
summary: The Court of Appeal of England and Wales has ruled against India in a dispute over whether a UAE investment authority can pursue arbitration over a failed bauxite mining project in Andhra Pradesh.The Court upheld an earlier ruling allowing Ras Al Khaimah Investment Authority (RAKIA) to proceed with its claims against India under the India-UAE Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT).A Bench of Lord Justices Males, Phillips and Miles dismissed India's appeal against a June 2025 judgment of the English High Court, which had overturned an arbitral tribunal's finding that it lacked jurisdiction to hear the dispute.The Court held that the government action directed at a company could qualify as action directly affecting a foreign investor's investment, even when the investment was held through a minority shareholding."It follows that, for the purposes of the BIT, a minority shareholding allocated to an Investor in exchange for capital investment in a company is not regarded as just an interest in the company," Lord Justice Phillips observed,The dispute arose from a 2007 memorandum of understanding between the Government of Andhra Pradesh and the Government of Ras Al Khaimah to establish an alumina refinery, aluminium smelter and power plant in Andhra Pradesh.RAKIA invested approximately $42.5 million in ANRAK Aluminium Limited, which was incorporated to implement the project. Its shareholding was subsequently diluted to approximately 12%.The project depended on bauxite supplies from the state-owned Andhra Pradesh Mineral Development Corporation (APMDC).However, following public protests, the Andhra Pradesh government reversed its position in 2015 and subsequently withdrew the orders authorising the bauxite supply arrangement. APMDC eventually terminated the supply agreement.RAKIA initiated arbitration against India in December 2016, alleging violations of the investment treaty, including failure to provide fair and equitable treatment and unlawful expropriation.In May 2022, an arbitral tribunal comprising Lord Hoffmann, Justice Chandramauli and J William Rowley QC ruled that it lacked jurisdiction.The tribunal reasoned that the government measures directly affected ANRAK and APMDC, while their impact on RAKIA's shareholding was merely indirect.However, Justice Robin Knowles of the English High Court overturned that finding in June 2025, prompting India's appeal.Before the Court of Appeal, India argued that RAKIA's protected investment consisted of its shares in ANRAK rather than the underlying aluminium project. Consequently, measures affecting the project or its supply arrangements could not be regarded as directly applied to RAKIA's investment.Rejecting this argument, the Court held that the treaty required investments to be understood in their economic context rather than merely as the legal instruments through which they were held."That reading of the BIT makes sense of and gives meaning to the protections given to Investments in its substantive provisions," the Court explained.It further observed that India's proposed interpretation could substantially undermine the protections contemplated under the treaty.The Court also rejected India's reliance on the circumstances surrounding the negotiation of the treaty, including India's response to the adverse arbitral award in White Industries v India.However, the Court disagreed with the High Court's suggestion that the distinction between direct and indirect application of government action depended on whether such action was specifically targeted at an investment.It clarified that the treaty excluded merely indirect or consequential effects of government action directed elsewhere.Applying this interpretation, the Court concluded,"I therefore agree with the Judge that the actions of the GoAP in the present case applied directly to RAKIA’s Investment."The Court held that the government's actions had ended the availability of the project's primary bauxite supply and led to the termination of the supply agreement.The dispute will now proceed before the tribunal for determination on merits as regards whether India breached the treaty or owes compensation to RAKIA.India was represented by Sam Wordsworth KC, Siddharth Dhar KC and Peter Webster, instructed by Dentons UK and Middle East LLP.RAKIA was represented by Tim Otty KC, Ben Juratowitch KC and Benedict Tompkins, instructed by Freshfields LLP.[Read Judgment]

title: Two routes to the same answer – The genericness plea in Noviets v. Novartis
summary: When a defendant in a trademark suit argues that a common element of its mark is generic to the trade, the response a court gives to that argument matters as much as the outcome. In Noviets Pharma v. Novartis AG (FAO(OS) (COMM) 143/2026), the defendants’ genericness plea over the prefix "NOV" was met first with a finding of estoppel: Noviets, having itself sought registration of "NOVIETS," was held disentitled to argue that "NOV" was common to trade. This piece asks whether that response was necessary, when an orthodox evidentiary route was available and had in fact been argued.The dispute concerns two pharmaceutical marks: "NOVARTIS," registered since 1996, and "NOVIETS," used by a set of interconnected entities dealing in pharmaceutical and veterinary products since around 2017–18. Novartis sought and obtained an interim injunction from the Single Judge in CS(COMM) 218/2024. Noviets appealed, and the Division bench dismissed the appeal, finding no perversity in the Single Judge's exercise of discretion under the Wander standard. The underlying suit remains pending trial before the Single Judge.The plea was that “NOV" is derived from "Nova" or "New" and is common to the pharmaceutical trade. The Single Judge held the defendants’ own registration application fatal to the plea: having applied to register “NOVIETS,” they could not contend that the prefix was common to trade, a party being unable to approbate and reprobate.AnalysisThe difficulty is that seeking the registration of a composite mark and arguing that one element within it is common to trade are not, on their own, inconsistent positions. Section 17(2) of the Act exists precisely because composite marks routinely contain such elements: registration of the whole confers no exclusive right over a part that is not separately registered or independently distinctive. A defendant who applied to register "NOVIETS" is not thereby representing that "NOV" alone is distinctive, only that the composite, taken as a whole, is capable of distinguishing its goods. A plea of genericness and a registration application therefore address different legal questions. Treating them as mutually destructive assumes a statutory inconsistency that does not exist.The authorities show the difficulty runs deeper. In Automatic Electric v. RK Dhawan the estoppel plea concerned ‘DIMMER” within the defendant’s own “DIMMER DOT” and in Ishi Khosla v. Anil Aggarwal, it concerned “Whole Foods” within the “DIET WHOLE FOODS.” Both authorities applied bar to a component and no to the whole mark. The single judge was following the settled principles of law, but so applied, the rule reaches exactly what Section 17(2) says a composite registration does not claim and leaves the defence available only to those who have filed nothing at all.Section 17(2) sits downstream of that evidentiary question rather than in place of it: it tells us what follows if NOV is shown to be common to the trade, not whether it is. The Division Bench, for its part, did not adopt the estoppel reasoning. At paragraph 36 it rejected the plea on the facts – use since 1996, turnover of INR 3,672 million – while correctly noting that Section 17 “protects the registered mark as a whole and limits exclusivity over individual components unless separately protected.” and then sustained a finding built entirely on a shared component i.e., “NOV”. The comparison was made by comparing NOV-AR-TIS and NOV-IE-TS instead of a holistic approach.In an intriguing analytical move, the Division Bench adroitly navigates existing pharmaceutical trademark jurisprudence by upholding a heightened, public-safety-oriented standard of confusion typically reserved for medicinal products. Specifically, paragraph 42 distinguishes landmark precedents like Cadila and Intas on the grounds that those disputes concerned drug brand names derived from active ingredients, rather than competing corporate marks. This dual approach exposes a critical doctrinal tension: to what extent should the strict health-risk threshold developed for look-alike or sound-alike medicines govern disputes exclusively involving corporate trade names operating within niche B2B channels?ConclusionNone of this is to suggest the outcome was wrong. Given Novartis's prior and bona fide use, its established reputation and goodwill, the genuine visual and phonetic closeness between "NOVARTIS" and "NOVIETS," and the absence of any explanation for how a coined mark so close to it was arrived at, the injunction was likely the right result on the facts. The argument here is narrower, testing the plea against what composite registration concedes, rather than deflecting it through estoppel, would have made the reasoning simpler and more self-sufficient, not different in outcome. The plea failed for want of evidence, and saying so would have been enough. Estoppel answered a question narrower than the one available and left behind a proposition wider than the facts required.About the author: Amit Panigrahi is a Partner, Samanyu Bhatnagar is a Senior Associate, and Ishikaa Seth is an Associate at Kochhar & Co.Disclaimer: The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author(s).
