title: Plea before Telangana High Court seeks publication of 1.16 lakh unpublished government orders
summary: A plea has been filed before the Telangana High Court alleging that the State government has failed to make public over 1.16 lakh Government Orders (GOs) issued since June 2014 despite earlier court directions to upload them online [B Vinay Reddy v The State of Telangana & Ors.].Filed by one B Vinay Reddy, the petition claims that the State government had informed the Telangana Legislative Assembly in March 2025 that 1,99,115 GOs had been issued between June 2, 2014 and March 14, 2025, of which only 82,657 were available in the public domain. As per the plea, 1,16,458 GOs or around 58.5 per cent are not publicly accessible.A subsequent response to an RTI application, dated November 18, 2025, showed that only 3,290 of the 19,064 GOs issued between December 7, 2023 and January 26, 2025 were available in the public domain.The plea is pending before Justice Surepalli Nanda.Justice Surepalli NandaThe plea alleges that the State government departments classify GOs as either 'public' or 'internal' on the Government Order Issue Register (GOIR) portal. It contends that departments withhold GOs without issuing reasoned orders citing Sections 8 or 9 of the RTI Act, which specify grounds for denying access to information. The petition argues that this practice prevents citizens from accessing government decisions that may affect their rights.As per the plea,“A Government Order which is kept out of the public domain cannot be known, obeyed, questioned or relied upon by the citizen whose rights it affects." The plea also refers to two earlier High Court orders passed on March 10, 2022 and December 23, 2025, directing the State to upload unpublished GOs within eight weeks. The petition submits that the directions have not been fully implemented.A contempt of court case concerning alleged non-compliance is also pending before the Court.The petitioner has sought directions from the High Court to the State government to publish all GOs issued since June 2, 2014, except those withheld for legally valid reasons. It also seeks disclosure of department-wise figures on unpublished orders, deadlines for uploading future orders and appointment of officers responsible for publishing them.The plea also challenges delays in responding to Reddy’s Right to Information (RTI) application filed on January 17, 2026, seeking year-wise and department-wise details of GOs issued and uploaded since 2014, reasons for non-publication and the rules governing it. The plea further alleges that the Telangana Information Commission took up Reddy's complaint, filed on February 22, only on July 15. It was heard three times without a decision and adjourned on October 13 without a next date being fixed. The petition also claims that the Commission had failed to provide hearing records or facilitate video-conference participation.“A body created to enforce transparency cannot withhold from a party the record of his own proceeding,” states the plea.The petition seeks directions to provide the requested RTI information free of cost within two weeks and decide his pending complaint within four weeks. It also seeks hybrid hearings, at least seven days’ advance notice of hearing dates and uploading of hearing records within three days.The plea was filed through advocate Mahesh Mamindla.

title: Delhi High Court rejects plea by Neha Bora against notice to sign bond and "maintain peace"
summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday dismissed a plea filed by All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora challenging a notice issued the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) directing Bora to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 and maintain peace.Justice Subramonium Prasad passed the order."Writ petition is rejected. However, there are certain directions give for the magistrate to take care of. All the material to be furnished to her," the Court said.The Court added that the magistrate [SEM] will also consider the import of Section 135 BNSS. “Whether 135 would warrant a production of the bond at the very first instance, or it's only during the course of the inquiries, and further incident take place, which gives the danger or not. These are matters the magistrate will take into account,” the court said.Justice Subramonium PrasadThe notice under challenge was issued by the Delhi Police to Bora on October 18, directing them to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) on October 19. It directed Bora to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 with a surety to “maintain peace during the period of inquiry” against them.According to Bora’s plea, the notice dated October 17 was issued by the SEM under Sections 126 and 130, read with Section 135(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), citing apprehensions of breach of public peace and tranquillity.Bora was detained on October 16 while attending a gathering at Mandi House. Bora alleged that they were taken to an undisclosed location and subsequently to RK Puram police station, where they were held overnight before being released at 6 AM the following day. They received the SEM notice on October 18.The notice cited allegations of sloganeering at Mandi House, repeated protests around Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, and allegedly instigating people to participate in a protest at Connaught Place.However, according to Bora's plea, the notice does not disclose any material establishing a likelihood of breach of peace or identify a specific event or period during which such a breach is apprehended.The petition also disputed the allegation concerning the Connaught Place protest. Bora argued that their call was for a peaceful gathering at Mandi House at 5 pm on October 16, where they were subsequently detained.Bora alleged that the proceedings amount to an attempt to curb peaceful dissent and violate their fundamental rights to freedom of speech, assembly and personal liberty.Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for Bora, submitted that all calls made by them were for peaceful protests."The facts are that over a period of time certain protests have arisen in the country as it the want against what the government does. As far as my client is concerned there has been no exhortation to violence it has been entirely peaceful. She has been asking for reforms. Over time, she has put out tweets and exhorted people to join," it was submitted.Sankaranarayanan referred to the press conference held by Bora on October 15 in response to the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as a protest site.He sought to distinguish the protest that happened at Connaught Place from the one which Bora had called for at Mandi House.Sankaranarayanan added that there is nothing wrong in making a call for a regime change in a democracy. Senior Advocate Gopal SankaranarayananHe also highlighted how the special executive magistrate issuing the notice is also a police officer."It is admitted that there was a direction by senior officers to initiate the procedure under Section 126. It is relevant because the SEM here is also an ACP," it was pointed out.He further flagged errors in the notice and maintained that no permission is required to hoist the national flag.Neha Bora No permission is needed to hoist the national flag.Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Chetan Sharma, appearing for Delhi Police, rebutted Bora's arguments. The ASG said that Section 126 and 130 of the BNSS have to be read together."If there is a likelihood that somebody may commit breach of peace, Section 126 BNSS kicks in with Section 130 BNSS. They can't be disjoined. Such technical splitting will take away the essence of public tranquillity and breach of peace," the ASG contended.ASG Chetan SharmaASG Sharma maintained that the notice was based on likelihood of breach of peace and cannot be assailed on the ground of technicality."Don't leave it to a technicality... All mayhem may have broken loose in the capital of the city. Because this is preventive in nature so that law would land its weight to the way parliament envisaged it to be," the ASG argued.Regarding Bora's arguments that the notice was factually incorrect since she was had not given any call for protest at Connaught Place but only at Mandi House, the ASG said,"Their argument that their call was only for Mandi House and not CP and that no 163 BNSS was in force is false. There was 163 BNSS. Police was outnumbered, she ran. She dodges. She was stopped, she did not stop. She ran towards CP."Besides Sankaranarayanan, advocates Abhik Chimni, Moksha Sharma, Ayan Dasgupta Samarendra, Pranjal Abrol and Gurupal Singh also appeared for Bora.ASG Chetan Sharma and CGSC Ashish Dixit represented the Delhi Police.

title: Legal tech in law firms and in-house teams: The wall is coming down
summary: For years, the legal technology market organised itself in a peculiar way. Law firms on one side, in-house legal teams on the other. Both bought legal tech, but rarely the same products. Legal research, document management and eDiscovery crossed over. Almost everything else split; the platforms were built around workflows pointing in opposite directions.The split made sense, because the two sides were buying for different outcomes. A firm sells expert time to external clients, so its technology existed to capture that time and protect the margin on it. Success meant utilisation and realisation. An in-house team is a business-enabler with one client - the business - and an ever-increasing queue of internal requests. The outcome it needs is the business moving safely with high velocity with as few lawyer hours as possible. Its work also doesn't end at signing: obligations and renewals run on for years. So technology that focuses on this side historically existed to route the volume and keep track of what happens after the deal closes.Firm tech made expert hours more valuable, whereas in-house tech aimed to make fewer of those hours necessary.That split is now breaking at one layer and hardening at another. The models are shared. The products built on them are starting to split again along the old line.The frontier model broke the wall (before vendors acted on it) Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT are used by law firms and in-house teams alike, often through enterprise deployments with no legal-specific wrapper. A partner drafting a memo and a general counsel stress-testing a contract position can be working in the same model, through the same interface. This matters because previous generations of legal technology were integration plays. They connected existing workflows, automated document flows and surfaced existing data in more useful formats. The intelligence, such as it was, lived mostly in the rules and structured data that humans had built around the system. The model itself was not the product. But that is changing. Frontier models can take on work that used to need a lawyer at every step. Of course, the output still needs real oversight, but it doesn't need rebuilding from scratch. When the same capability serves an associate and in-house counsel doing comparable work, the case for two separate product markets gets thin.But what about the core legaltech vendors? This play is most visible at the platform layer. Harvey launched as a law firm tool and is now a fixture in in-house environments. Luminance built its reputation in law firm due diligence and has expanded steadily into CLM and legal operations. Legora sells one platform to both, but is now building segment-specific products on top of it. The companies themselves rarely frame this as convergence; they frame it as expansion.This is partly commercial. Law firms and in-house teams are both large buyers and serving only one side of the relationship is a constraint, not a strategy. But it is also a product decision, because the underlying tasks are not as different as the market structure implied. Contract analysis looks similar whether the lawyer doing it sits in a firm or a legal department. So does due diligence, drafting, regulatory review, issue spotting. The divide was shrinking before the legal tech vendors had fully registered it.Shared engine, separate front doors The legal AI tools may be shared, but how law firms and in-house departments use it in their workflows are completely different.Law firms operate around matters: defined engagements with starts, ends, billing codes and client reporting. In-house legal teams operate around continuous flows of work with no natural beginning, internal stakeholders instead of paying clients and obligations that run across time rather than project. These are not just organisational differences. They reflect genuinely different ways of thinking about how legal work is structured.An in-house team using a platform built around matter logic will encounter assumptions that do not map onto how their work flows. A law firm using a platform built around operational throughput will find itself reaching for structures the product did not anticipate. Capability has converged faster than workflow design has. The platforms are still working out what a genuinely shared model of legal work looks like when you are not starting from an assumption about which institutional context it sits inside.October 2026 showed how vendors are answering that. In the same week, Legora and Harvey each launched a product called Intake. Each is a front door for in-house teams that captures requests, asks for missing context, routes work to the right lawyer and drafts a first pass from the team’s own playbooks. Legora’s is live in Slack. Harvey’s is in early access. Both are built for legal departments, not firms. The engine is shared and the product on top of it is splitting along the old line. None of this is new. The previous generation of legal tech didn't just segment the market, but encoded the split. Firms bought practice management and billing built around engagements with a paying client. Legal departments bought the mirror image: matter management and e-billing built to control spend on those same engagements. Same matter, opposite ends of the invoice.CLM’s problem is that the AI platforms are coming in-house Contract lifecycle management (CLM) is the clearest case. These systems were built entirely around in-house legal operations: intake portals, approval workflows, obligation tracking, renewal calendars. Law firms have no native use of CLM, but at times offer it as a managed service to clients.For years, the threat to CLM vendors looked distant, because legal AI platforms were law firm tools. That’s no longer true. The platforms that won the firms are now selling directly to legal departments and they’re taking pieces of the CLM stack with them. Take contract redlining. A firm associate reviewing a counterparty's MSA and an in-house counsel handling an incoming NDA can each load a playbook and fallback positions into Spellbook or Harvey inside Word and get speedy redlines, with comments explaining each change. The only difference is whose playbook it is. For the firm, it belongs to the client and for the in-house team, it belongs to the company.Obligation tracking follows the same pattern through tabular extraction. A firm running diligence on a deal and a legal department auditing its own executed agreements can both drop a batch of contracts into Harvey Vault or Legora's Tabular Review. Each gets a grid with one row per contract and columns for renewal dates, notice periods, payment terms and audit rights.Intake goes further. Harvey’s version routes contract work into its own Contract Intelligence product. That looks less like a workaround to CLM and more like a bid to become it.The legacy vendors built their moats around the assumption that the two markets would stay separate. Legal AI platforms are making that assumption look increasingly fragile.Clients now know what the work takes Firms have long operated on the basis that they knew what work required what expertise, how long it took and what it was worth. Clients accepted that framing because they lacked a credible alternative. An in-house team using the same platform as their outside counsel starts to develop real intuitions about how long document review should take, what contract analysis actually involves and where human judgment adds value versus where it is reconstructing work the platform could have done faster. Those intuitions enter conversations about scope, budgets and billing. They change what clients feel entitled to ask.The bigger shift is in information, more than fees. When both parties in a professional services relationship are working within the same technological frame, the knowledge gap that historically structured that relationship starts to close. What gets renegotiated is not just cost. It is the definition of the service itself.Nobody has worked out how juniors learn to supervise The law firm model has always depended on a specific learning architecture. Junior lawyers do structured work - research, drafting, review - and develop judgment through repetition and feedback. That judgment eventually becomes what clients pay senior rates for. It works because the early work is meaningful in both output and developmental terms.If a platform handles first-pass contract review as well as a junior associate, the question is not just what the associate does instead. It is how the associate develops the judgment to supervise and refine the platform's work without having done the underlying task enough times to know what it feels like to get it wrong. Supervision without prior experience is a different skill and the profession has not yet worked out how to build it.In-house teams face an adjacent version and it’s no longer hypothetical. Legora’s Intake can complete pre-approved routine requests end-to-end and send the answer straight back to the business. Harvey’s platform resolves routine requests and drafts the rest. A lawyer reviewing that output is working on what to remove from the material. That’s often efficient. It can also slowly wear away the close engagement that makes oversight mean something. The risk is that lawyers stop knowing what they’re looking for.Accountability has not caught up with the platforms Traditional legal technology came with a defined responsibility map. The vendor supplied the tool, the organisation implemented it and the lawyer remained professionally accountable for the work product. That held because the tool was doing something discrete and bounded: retrieving a document, surfacing a clause, flagging a deadline.Platforms operating across both environments are doing something more continuous. They shape how work is initiated, scoped, analysed and delivered. The lawyer remains accountable, but the platform is increasingly embedded in the chain of decisions that leads to the output the lawyer signs off on. When something goes wrong, the question of where the error entered the process is genuinely difficult to answer. The legal profession has governance frameworks developed over a very long time for very good reasons. The question is not whether they apply here. It is what they look like when the assistance is this deeply embedded in the work itself.The wall was never natural and it’s being rebuilt The fault line that organised the legal technology market for decades was never natural. It was a product of how technology was built, how professional services relationships were structured and how the economics of legal work had historically developed. None of that was permanent. It was contingent.What the current generation of Legal AI platforms is doing, more than anything else, is making that contingency visible. The harder questions - who captures the value that gets displaced, how expertise develops in this new architecture, where professional accountability sits when a platform is this embedded in legal work - are not going to be resolved by the technology itself. They require the profession to make active choices about what it is actually for.Those conversations are beginning, but they're running well behind what's shifting. The sharpest one: if clients learn what the work takes and juniors stop doing it, who gets paid for the judgment that's left? Shreya Vajpei is the Founder of Indian LegalTech Network.Vaishali Gopal is Senior Advisor, Indian LegalTech Network and Founder of Future Relics Consulting.

title: SEM notice asking Neha Bora to sign peace bond not based on mere hearsay: Delhi High Court
summary: The Delhi High Court on Friday observed that the show-cause notice issued by a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) to All India Students Association (AISA) president Neha Bora to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 and maintain peace was not based on mere "hearsay". Justice Subramonium Prasad observed that the notice was based on the kalandara dated October 17, which consists of the three general diary entries registered at different police stations related to different dates and events. "As such, this Court cannot sit in the armchair of the SEM to test the subjective satisfaction of the sufficiency of material and as to whether the opinion has been correctly been arrived at by the SEM or not," the Bench said. The Court said that the notice, issued under Sections 126 and 130 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), met the legal requirements for initiating preventive proceedings.The High Court arrived at these findings while dismissing Bora's plea against the notice. However, the Court directed the police to provide all the material to Bora on which reliance will be placed at the time of enquiry and on which basis the notice has been issued. "The SEM is also directed to ensure that the principles of natural justice are not violated before passing any order directing furnishing of a bond," the Court ordered. It clarified that the SEM must independently assess the material before deciding whether Bora should be directed to furnish a bond during the inquiry. "This Court, however, deems it fit to state that the SEM must necessarily keep in mind the import of Section 135 of the BNSS and leaves it open for the SEM to decide on the insistence of a bond at the first instance, as the provision provides for furnishing a bond only if there is an apprehension of breach of peace or disturbance after the commencement and before the completion of the enquiry," the Court said. Justice Subramonium PrasadThe notice under challenge was issued by the Delhi Police to Bora on October 18, directing them to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) on October 19.
